messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Delivery Driver
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 46

**Case Vignette: "Raj"**

Raj is a 34-year-old South Asian man who works as a delivery driver for a national courier service. He has been married for six years and lives with his wife and their two young children in a suburban apartment. He presents for therapy at the urging of his wife, who has noticed a profound change in him over the past eight months.

The event that changed everything happened on a rainy Tuesday afternoon in late November. Raj was making his usual route, running slightly behind schedule. He remembers the windshield wipers struggling against the downpour, the way the streetlights reflected off the wet asphalt. He was approaching an intersection when the light turned yellow. He pressed the gas, trying to beat it. He didn't see the man crossing until it was too late. The impact wasn't loud—it was more of a dull thud, followed by the sickening screech of brakes that weren't his own. He remembers the paramedics asking him questions he couldn't answer, the way his hands shook as he tried to call his wife, the hospital waiting room with its flickering fluorescent lights. The man survived, but with a traumatic brain injury and a shattered leg. He will likely never walk the same again.

In the weeks that followed, Raj stopped sleeping. He would lie in bed, replaying the moment over and over—the yellow light, the pressure of his foot on the gas, the fraction of a second where he could have stopped but didn't. He started avoiding driving. He took unpaid leave from work, telling his supervisor he was sick. The thought of getting behind the wheel made his chest tighten, his palms sweat. His wife drove him to the grocery store, to his parents' house, to the children's school. He couldn't even look at the delivery van parked in the lot without feeling a wave of nausea.

The nightmares began about a month after the accident. They are always the same: he is driving, the road is wet, and a figure appears in front of the van. He tries to brake, but the pedal is made of rubber, useless. He wakes up gasping, his heart pounding, convinced he has just killed someone. His wife has learned to sleep with the lights on because he wakes up disoriented, sometimes crying, sometimes screaming.

At work, he has been reassigned to the warehouse, but even there, the sound of reversing trucks or the screech of tires in the loading bay makes him flinch. He has become hypervigilant. He checks his mirrors obsessively when his wife drives. He walks with his shoulders hunched, scanning the ground in front of him. He has stopped riding his bicycle, a hobby he once loved. He tells his therapist that he feels like a ghost haunting his own life.

His relationships have suffered. He is irritable with his children, snapping at them for small noises. He has withdrawn from his wife, unable to explain the shame he feels. He avoids family gatherings, afraid someone will ask about work or driving. He has started drinking most evenings—just a few beers, he says, to quiet his mind enough to sleep. But the sleep never comes easily.

He describes a constant, low-grade guilt that feels like a weight on his chest. He thinks about the man he hit, wonders if he has a family, if he can work, if he will ever forgive himself. He has stopped making plans for the future. When his wife talks about taking a vacation next summer, he feels a hollow dread. He cannot imagine a time when this feeling will be gone. He has started to believe that he does not deserve to feel better.

He is here today because his wife told him she is worried he is disappearing. He doesn't disagree. He just doesn't know how to find his way back.
